name: S-23

lead: S-23 is an experimental selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed by GTx, Inc. as a possible male hormonal contraceptive. It binds the androgen receptor more tightly than the older SARM andarine.
Its appearance relevance comes from the broader SARM category, which is used in muscle-building circles. No human trials of S-23 are described in the sources consulted.

paras: It is a nonsteroidal compound that binds the androgen receptor (reported Ki of about 1.7 nM). In animal work it was reported to suppress spermatogenesis in a dose-dependent way, with recovery after treatment stopped.

No human safety data are described. SARMs as a class are banned by WADA, and compounds sold online as research chemicals have been reported to be mislabeled. Class-level reports include liver enzyme elevation and suppression of the body's own testosterone production.

lead: S-23 (also called Mastorin) is an investigational selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed by GTx, Inc. as a candidate male hormonal contraceptive.[1] It is a nonsteroidal compound that binds the androgen receptor with higher affinity than the older SARM andarine.[1]

Animal studies reported in the literature summarised on Wikipedia describe a favourable ratio of anabolic to androgenic effects and dose-dependent suppression of sperm production that recovered after treatment ended.[1] The sources consulted describe no published human trials. It was reported as a novel designer drug by 2020.[1]
infobox: Investigational New Drug (US); SARMs as a class are prohibited by WADA

paras: No studies found. Related research is limited to animal work on contraception and to studies of other SARMs, such as enobosarm, which a Phase III trial found increased lean body mass without a significant improvement in physical function.[2]
S-23 binds the androgen receptor with a reported Ki of 1.7 nM.[1]

SARMs as a class were prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency in 2008.[2] Small laboratories sell SARMs online as research chemicals, and products have been reported to be mislabeled.[2] Class-level adverse effects described in the literature include raised liver enzymes, lower HDL cholesterol and suppression of testosterone, with case reports of liver injury in recreational users.[2] S-23 itself is listed as an Investigational New Drug in the United States.[1]
